description: We are a team of 4 passionate engineers, we like to build stuff.
summary:
DeepFrost Bridge is our project for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We search Earth for places where drilling can be tested in conditions similar to those on Mars, in ground that holds ice like the ground under candidate Mars base sites. The match does not have to be exact. Permafrost also does not have to last all year, only be frozen at a given time of year. The system combines permafrost data (Global Permafrost Zonation Index, ESA Permafrost CCI) with NASA data: ground temperature, depth to permafrost, dryness (SMAP), and exposed bare ground (MODIS). Each grid cell is scored, checked for stability, and grouped into areas with a suggested drilling point. An interactive 3D app shows the results.

This matters because drilling is how future missions will look for water on Mars: its ground ice is the most accessible water source for a crewed base. Testing drilling equipment and methods on Earth, in conditions close to Mars, lets teams prepare before a mission is sent.
details:
The problem
At every candidate Mars site, ground ice sits under a dry cover, never thaws, and lies in ground colder than anywhere on Earth. A drill that works there has to be tested first. Earth cannot match Mars pressure, gravity, radiation or its roughly 200 K ground, so the project does not look for Earth places that are "closest" to Mars in every number. It looks for places that match the conditions Earth can actually reproduce.

How it works
1. Mask. We check 401,614 permafrost cells on Earth, each 0.1° across, taken from the Global Permafrost Zonation Index, with the ESA Permafrost CCI in Antarctica.
2. Filter. About 53,000 cells pass the filters: ground at or below −5 °C at the drilling depth, summer thaw no deeper than 0.5 m, bare ground present in summer, and not mostly covered by glacier or ice sheet.
3. Score. Each remaining cell is scored against each of the 7 candidate Mars base sites. Which features count depends on the depth layer. Near the surface (0–1 m) they are summer surface temperature compared with the Mars site, dryness and bare ground. Deeper down (1–5 m and below 5 m) they include how cold the ground is at that depth.
4. Test stability. Each scored cell is re-tested under up to 16 variants of the thresholds and features, to make sure its place in the ranking does not depend on a single choice.
5. Suggest a site. The top cells are grouped into areas of at most 5 × 5 cells, and the best cell of each area is the suggested drilling point.

Results
Most of the best matches are in Antarctica and Greenland. This is expected: their cold, dry polar deserts are the closest match to Mars on Earth, and they include well-known Mars analogs such as the McMurdo Dry Valleys. We also wanted to find places beyond these obvious ones, and the results include two more: the north of Canada, which is among the top matches for every Mars base site, and the Andes, which closely match the warmer Hellas rim site.
